Buffet has three distinct meanings as a noun. Two are very common; one is mostly literary.
Meaning 1 — A style of serving food (most common)

A buffet is a way of presenting and eating a meal where all the food is laid out on a long table or counter in advance, and guests walk along it, serve themselves whatever they want, in whatever quantity they like, and then sit down to eat.

The defining idea is self-service with free choice. Unlike a regular restaurant where a waiter brings you specific dishes you ordered, at a buffet the food is simply there, on display, available to everyone. You pick up a plate, walk along the spread, and put whatever catches your eye onto your plate. You can return for second or third helpings as many times as you want.

What a typical buffet looks like in practice:

  • A long table or counter lined with trays and dishes of food, kept warm under lamps or in heated containers.
  • A wide variety of foods all available at the same time — starters, main dishes, sides, salads, desserts — so you can eat a little of everything or a lot of just one thing.
  • Usually a single fixed price to enter, after which you can eat as much as you want. This is why buffets are often described as "all-you-can-eat."
  • Plates, tongs, and serving spoons are provided for you to serve yourself.

Where you'll encounter buffets:

  • Buffet restaurants — entire restaurants designed around this model, very common in Indian, Chinese, and American dining culture.
  • Hotel breakfast buffets — where the morning meal is displayed for all staying guests.
  • Wedding and party buffets — instead of a sit-down meal with a fixed menu, guests serve themselves from a shared spread.
  • Office events and catering — food laid out for a gathering or celebration.
  • Buffet cars on trains — a small counter or section on a train where passengers walk up and pick snacks, sandwiches, or drinks. (Also called a "buffet car" or "dining car.")

You'll commonly hear phrases like "breakfast buffet," "lunch buffet," "dinner buffet," or "buffet spread" — all variations that simply tell you which meal is being served in this style, or emphasize the generousness of the spread.

The core idea always stays the same: food is presented communally, you help yourself, there's variety, and you're not confined to a single fixed serving.

A buffet is also a specific type of furniture found in a dining room. It is a long, wide, flat-topped wooden cabinet that sits against the wall — roughly at waist height. It has drawers and enclosed cupboard sections inside for storing dining room items: plates, glasses, cutlery, serving bowls, tablecloths, and so on.

Its flat top surface is particularly useful during meals — dishes can be placed on it for easy access when serving, which is where the connection to the food meaning comes from. In many homes, the buffet doubles as a display surface, where decorative objects or a vase of flowers might sit on top when the table is not in use.

You may also hear it called a sideboard — the two words are often used interchangeably, though some people use "sideboard" for a slightly taller or more formal version. Visually, imagine a long, sturdy chest of drawers but wider, lower, and designed specifically for the dining room.

In older and more formal English, buffet as a noun means a sharp, forceful blow or knock — most often from a natural force like wind, waves, or rain, rather than a deliberate human punch.

For example: "The explorers endured the buffets of the freezing wind." Here, "buffets" means repeated harsh blows or impacts from the wind.

This meaning is rarely used in everyday modern conversation. You are most likely to encounter it in literature, formal prose, or older texts. It is worth knowing so you are not confused when you come across it in reading, but you would not typically use it yourself when speaking.

| (not a table — just a clear recap) |
When someone says "Let's go to a buffet," they mean a self-serve meal spread.
When someone points to furniture and says "the buffet," they mean a low dining-room cabinet.
When a novel says "the buffets of fate," it means repeated harsh blows.

The first meaning is by far the most commonly used in daily life.
